A000040  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true, and it is the degenerate case of a general fact about power maps on a squarefree modulus: for P = p_1*...*p_k the image of the e-th power map on (Z/PZ)* is a subgroup of order Prod_i (p_i - 1)/gcd(e, p_i - 1), and membership in that image characterises coprimality to P. Detlefs' exponent f(n) = lcm(p_1-1, ..., p_n-1) makes that image trivial, which is what produces the clean congruence k^f(n) = 1 (mod P). - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A000071  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true. The sequence itself is not a strong divisibility sequence -- gcd(a(4), a(6)) = 1 while a(gcd(4,6)) = a(2) = 0 -- but restricting the index to a fixed odd geometric progression makes it one. For odd j, F(j) - 1 = F(E)*L(O), where E and O are the even and the odd member of the pair {(j-1)/2, (j+1)/2}; along j = k^n the two indices inherit the cyclotomic gcd structure of k^n -/+ 1, which is exactly what a strong divisibility sequence needs. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A000139  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true. By Legendre's formula the parity of a(n) is decided by s(2n+1) + s(n+1) - s(3n) = 1 for the binary digit sum s; writing t for the number of trailing 1s of n and counting the carries in the binary addition n + 2n gives the identity exactly when n is an odd Fibbinary number. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A047926  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true once an off-by-one in the indexing is corrected: for every k >= 1 the number of representations of 9^k as a^2 + b^2 + c^2 with 0 < a <= b <= c is (3^k + 2^k - 1)/4 = a(k-1), not a(k). More precisely, exactly k of them have two equal parts and (3^k - 2^k - 1)/4 have three distinct parts; none has three equal parts, and 9^k is never a sum of two positive squares. The argument deflates Pall's classical count r_3(9^k) = 6*(2*3^k - 1) to unordered positive triples, the two degenerate shapes being controlled by the divisor counts attached to x^2 + y^2 and x^2 + 2y^2, both of class number one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A051560  A proof of the conjectured recurrence for OEIS A051560

A052895  The reduction of OEIS A052895 modulo $k$:\\ a proof that the period divides $\varphi(k)$

A059324  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true, and the sharper statement holds: such a pair (p, q) exists if and only if 6n + 5 is prime, and then it is unique in its first coordinate, namely p = 3 and q = 6n + 5. So this sequence is exactly the set of n >= 1 admitting no such pair. The reason is elementary: every prime p >= 5 has p^2 = 1 (mod 6), which forces 3 | q and hence q = 3, contradicting q > p^2. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A061002  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true, and it is a restatement of Wolstenholme's theorem rather than merely a consequence of it: the identity holds for a prime p exactly when p^2 divides the numerator of H_(p-1). Writing H_(p-1) = A/B in lowest terms, the two quantities in the quotient are exactly p*A and A/p^2, and the p^2 in the second is the whole content. The restriction p > 3 is therefore not cosmetic: at p = 2 and p = 3 the quotient is 2 and 9, not 8 and 27. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A063081  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: Conjectured: G.f.: x\^{}2*(x\^{}4 + x\^{}3 + 4*x\^{}2 + 5*x + 3)/(x\^{}5 -x\^{}3 -x\^{}2 +1). (End)
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 8 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A063168  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(x\^{}2 + 22*x + 7)/(x - 1)\^{}2 (conjectured). (End)
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 8 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A092287  The prime factorisation of a rectangular product of gcds:\\ a proof of Kaydalov's conjecture on OEIS A

A129365  A closed form for the $p$-adic valuation of OEIS A,\\ and a proof that its terms are integers
    NOTE: Conjectures B and C were given proofs in Aug 2026 (Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941, now linked on the entry); the draft claims A and D and only mentions that B and C follow
    conjecture: \textbf{Conjectures:} A) $a(n)$ is always an integer.
Conjecture A is true, and more: for every prime p, ord_p(a(n)) = Sum_{i>=1} B(floor(n/p^i)) with B(M) = Sum_{k=1..M} (M mod k) = A004125(M). A sum of remainders is nonnegative, so every exponent is, which gives A; the formula is Conjecture D, and B and C follow from it as well. The proof is the known factorisation of the numerator, the identity floor(n/(k*p^i)) = floor(floor(n/p^i)/k) for the denominator, and M^2 - Sum_{k<=M} k*floor(M/k) = Sum_{k<=M} (M mod k). - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A140901  The empirical product formula for OEIS A140901, proved
    conjecture: (Empirical) Set p,q,r to n,5,3 (in any order) in s=p+q+r-1; a(n) = Product\_{i=0..r-1} (binomial(s,p+i)*i!/(s-i)\^{}(r-i-1)). (Conjecture) G.f.: (1 + 40*x + 400
The empirical formula is true. Reverse the rows and the columns: a matrix over 0..n that is nondecreasing along rows and down columns becomes one that is nonincreasing, which is exactly a plane partition with parts at most n inside a P X Q rectangle -- so a(n) counts the plane partitions in a P X Q X n box, which is the formula already noted on this entry. That triple product telescopes in its third index, leaving a(n) = Product_{i=1..P} Product_{j=1..Q} (n+i+j-1)/(i+j-1), a polynomial in n of degree P*Q. Clearing the denominator of the empirical expression then turns it into an identity between two polynomials whose degrees are bounded by inspection, so checking it at that many points settles it. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

Clearing the denominator of the empirical expression then turns it into an identity between two polynomials whose degrees are bounded by inspection, so checking it at that many points settles it. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A180752  An element and the cells around it: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 2*a(n-1) + a(n-2) - a(n-3) - a(n-5).
The empirical recurrence is true. Every cell the condition names lies a bounded number of lines away -- two of them, where it reaches a knight's move -- so a window of that width decides the condition on the line in the middle, and the lines with nothing far enough beyond them are decided at the end. Counting a line at a time therefore gives a transfer matrix with 7 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 5. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A183452  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A183452, proved
    conjecture: Conjecture: g.f. -x*(1 +5*x +607360*x\^{}20 -11532*x\^{}9 +753306*x\^{}19 +6*x\^{}2 -288*x\^{}26 -57080*x\^{}10 -612804*x\^{}16 +7234*x\^{}8 -600857*x\^{}17 +18
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 1 056 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A183645  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A183645, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(325 - 3874*x + 16055*x\^{}2 - 26930*x\^{}3 + 15000*x\^{}4) / ((1 - x)*(1 - 2*x)*(1 - 3*x)*(1 - 4*x)*(1 - 5*x)). - \_Colin Barker\_, Apr 01 2018
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 125 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A184130  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A184130, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(2 - x)*(3 - 11*x + 28*x\^{}2 - 42*x\^{}3 + 39*x\^{}4 - 22*x\^{}5 + 7*x\^{}6 - x\^{}7) / (1 - x)\^{}9.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 18 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A185369  A proof of the conjectured recurrence for OEIS A185369
    conjecture: \small \textbf{Conjecture:} +2*a(n) +4*(-n+1)*a(n-1) +2*(n-1)*(n-3)*a(n-2) +(n-1)*(n-2)*a(n-3)=0.
The e.g.f. above is not algebraic, but it lies in a finitely generated module over Q(x) spanned by powers of a logarithm times powers of an exponential, and that module is closed under differentiation, so a(n) is P-recursive. Reducing the conjectured operator inside it leaves a polynomial, and the recurrence holds for n > 3. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A188707  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A188707, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(5 - 4*x)/(1 - 5*x + 3*x\^{}2). - \_Colin Barker\_, Mar 11 2012
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 8 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A194932  The empirical closed form and generating function for OEIS A194932, proved
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 171*n - 127 for n>2. Empirical g.f.: x*(64 + 89*x + 16*x\^{}2 + 2*x\^{}3) / (1 - x)\^{}2. - \_Colin Barker\_, May 05 2018
This is true, and it is exact rather than eventual guesswork. The shape is fixed and it is the alphabet 0..n that grows, so this is not a walk count. The condition only ever compares two entries, so adding a constant to every entry keeps an array admissible: the arrays fall into translation classes, and a class whose largest and smallest entries differ by s contributes max(0, n+1-s) arrays with entries in 0..n. There are finitely many classes, because any two cells are joined by a path of at most D edges and each edge moves the value by at most d, so no class has s > d*D. For n at least that bound every term is positive and a(n) is exactly linear, so computing a(n) at two points fixes it for good. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A202048  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A202048, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 12*x*(53 - 207*x + 380*x\^{}2 - 398*x\^{}3 + 245*x\^{}4 - 83*x\^{}5 + 12*x\^{}6) / (1 - x)\^{}7.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 157 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A203175  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A203175, proved
    conjecture: Empirical G.f.: -x*(1+x\^{}2) / ( -1+x+2*x\^{}3 ). - \_R. J. Mathar\_, Jul 02 2013
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 12 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A205219  Arrays counted up to renaming: the empirical recurrence for OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = a(n-1) +4*a(n-2).
The empirical recurrence is true. Counting the arrays a line at a time gives a transfer matrix: the subblock condition looks only at a bounded window of consecutive lines, and "new values introduced in row major order" -- which is not a condition on any window, since it counts colourings up to renaming -- enters only through how many values have been introduced so far, one extra integer in the state. That gives 3 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 2. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A205248  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A205248, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 8*x*(2 - 3*x)/((1 - x)*(1 - 3*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 8 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A206163  Arrays counted up to renaming: the empirical recurrence for OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = a(n-1) + 217*a(n-2) - 33*a(n-3) - 1320*a(n-4) - 432*a(n-5) + 1152*a(n-6) for n>7.
The empirical recurrence is true. Counting the arrays a line at a time gives a transfer matrix: the subblock condition looks only at a bounded window of consecutive lines, and "new values introduced in row major order" -- which is not a condition on any window, since it counts colourings up to renaming -- enters only through how many values have been introduced so far, one extra integer in the state. Each column counts arrays of a fixed width, and counting those a row at a time gives a transfer matrix, so every column satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most the number of states; checking the ones above is then a finite exact computation, and they hold. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A206377  Arrays counted up to renaming: the empirical recurrence for OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 36*a(n-1) - 377*a(n-2) + 1398*a(n-3) - 2064*a(n-4) + 1008*a(n-5).
The empirical recurrence is true. Counting the arrays a line at a time gives a transfer matrix: the subblock condition looks only at a bounded window of consecutive lines, and "new values introduced in row major order" -- which is not a condition on any window, since it counts colourings up to renaming -- enters only through how many values have been introduced so far, one extra integer in the state. That gives 12 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 5. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A206839  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A206839, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 1 / (1 - 4*x + 2*x\^{}3 - x\^{}4). - \_Colin Barker\_, Jul 05 2019
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 21 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

    conjecture: G.f.: 9*x*(1 + 5*x - 2*x\^{}2) / (1 - x)\^{}4.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 91 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A207106  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A207106, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 2*x*(3 + 6*x - 5*x\^{}2) / (1 - x)\^{}4.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 43 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A207449  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A207449, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 10*x*(1 + 6*x - x\^{}2) / (1 - x)\^{}4.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 111 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A207596  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A207596, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 15*x*(1 + 11*x + x\^{}2 - x\^{}3) / (1 - x)\^{}4.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 241 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A208347  An element and the cells around it: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 10*a(n-1) -9*a(n-2) for n>4
The empirical recurrence is true. Every cell the condition names lies a bounded number of lines away -- two of them, where it reaches a knight's move -- so a window of that width decides the condition on the line in the middle, and the lines with nothing far enough beyond them are decided at the end. Counting a line at a time therefore gives a transfer matrix with 5 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 4. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A208375  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A208375, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 10*x*(1 + 7*x - 3*x\^{}2 - x\^{}3) / (1 - x)\^{}3.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 111 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A210474  A proof of the conjectured recurrence for OEIS A210474
    conjecture: \small \textbf{Conjecture:} (n+1)*a(n) +2*(-5*n+3)*a(n-1) +9*(n-3)*a(n-2)=0. - \emph{R. J. Mathar}, Jun 14 2016

A210781  A value repeated at its own distance: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = a(n-2) +2*a(n-3) +4*a(n-4) +38*a(n-5) +106*a(n-6) +172*a(n-7) +596*a(n-8) +573*a(n-9) +971*a(n-10) +744*a(n-11) -1425*a(n-12) -4335*a(n-13) -1
The empirical recurrence is true. The condition ranges over the whole array but reaches only as far as the value itself, which the alphabet bounds, so carrying that many lines together with one bit per cell -- has this cell found its partner yet -- makes the count a walk count on 99 states. Hence a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and checking the one above is a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 51. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A218348  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A218348, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(3 + 2*x + 2*x\^{}2 - 2*x\^{}3 - x\^{}4)/(1 - 3*x - 2*x\^{}2 - 2*x\^{}3 + x\^{}4 + x\^{}5). - \_Andrew Howroyd\_, May 10 2017
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 21 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A220563  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A220563, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(1 + 3*x - x\^{}3) / ((1 + x)*(1 - 3*x - x\^{}2 + x\^{}3)). - \_Colin Barker\_, Jul 31 2018
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 5 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A221394  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: Empirical g.f.: x\^{}2*(18 - 233*x\^{}2 + 820*x\^{}4 - 1050*x\^{}6 + 412*x\^{}8 + 46*x\^{}10) / ((1 - x)*(1 + x)*(1 - 47*x\^{}2 + 393*x\^{}4 - 605*x\^{}6 + 268*
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 348 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A223056  A global condition that is really a local one: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 18*a(n-1) - 71*a(n-2) + 102*a(n-3) - 48*a(n-4) for n>5.
The empirical recurrence is true. The condition is stated about connected sets of equal values, but a connected set fails to lie in a straight line exactly when it contains a turn -- a cell with an equal neighbour beside it and an equal neighbour above or below it -- since a connected set with both a horizontal and a vertical join has two consecutive joins of different kinds, and they share such a cell. Whether a cell has an equal neighbour beside it is decided by its own row, so the whole condition is a condition on pairs of adjacent rows, and counting a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 5 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 5. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A223211  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A223211, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 6*x*(1 + x) / (1 - 2*x - 4*x\^{}2).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 6 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A223382  A global condition that is really a local one: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 19*a(n-1) - 72*a(n-2) + 34*a(n-3) + 44*a(n-4) for n>5.
The empirical recurrence is true. The condition is stated about connected sets of equal values, but a connected set fails to lie in a straight line exactly when it contains a turn -- a cell with an equal neighbour beside it and an equal neighbour above or below it -- since a connected set with both a horizontal and a vertical join has two consecutive joins of different kinds, and they share such a cell. Whether a cell has an equal neighbour beside it is decided by its own row, so the whole condition is a condition on pairs of adjacent rows, and counting a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 5 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 5. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 312 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. A225007  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A225007, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1 + 10*x + 5*x\^{}2) / (1 - x)\^{}6. (End)
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 16 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A225311  A lattice count, not a walk count: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = a(n-1) + a(n-2) - 2*a(n-5) + a(n-8) + a(n-9) - a(n-10).
The empirical recurrence is true, and the arrays can be dispensed with entirely. A nondecreasing row of -1s and 1s is a block of -1s followed by a block of 1s, so it is fixed by one number k_i, the count of -1s; the row sums to n - 2k_i and the condition Sum_{i,j} i*x(i,j) = 0 becomes Sum_i i*k_i = n*H*(H+1)/4. So a(n) counts the lattice points of the box {0..n}^H on one hyperplane -- the points of the n-th dilate of a fixed rational polytope -- and is therefore a quasi-polynomial in n. A quasi-polynomial of degree d and period P satisfies the recurrence with characteristic polynomial (x^P - 1)^(d+1); here d <= H-1 and P divides 2*lcm(1..H), so the order is at most 96. Checking the recurrence above against that bound is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 9. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A230647  The white squares of a board: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 9*a(n-2) -4*a(n-4).
The empirical recurrence is true. Only the cells with i+j even carry a value, and the diagonal and antidiagonal neighbours of such a cell are again such cells, so the white squares form a board of their own on which the condition looks one line up and one line down. Three consecutive lines therefore settle it for the middle one, and counting a line at a time gives a transfer matrix with 5 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 4. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A230691  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 94 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 152 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Its order is 94, the order stated here, and so is the order of every tail. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A230942  The white squares of a board: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 3*a(n-1) + 14*a(n-3) + a(n-4) - a(n-5).
The empirical recurrence is true. Only the cells with i+j even carry a value, and the diagonal and antidiagonal neighbours of such a cell are again such cells, so the white squares form a board of their own on which the condition looks one line up and one line down. Three consecutive lines therefore settle it for the middle one, and counting a line at a time gives a transfer matrix with 9 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 2. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A232042  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A232042, proved
    conjecture: Empirical g.f.: x*(4 - x - 16*x\^{}2 - 5*x\^{}3 + 12*x\^{}4) / (1 - 4*x - 9*x\^{}2 + x\^{}3 + 6*x\^{}4). - \_Colin Barker\_, Oct 02 2018
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 50 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A232582  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A232582, proved
    conjecture: Empirical: G.f.: -2*x\^{}2 / ( -1+2*x-x\^{}2+x\^{}3 ). - \_R. J. Mathar\_, Nov 23 2014
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 90 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A233017  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 33 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 71 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Its order is 33, the order stated here, and so is the order of every tail. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A233085  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A233085, proved by carrying a row major clause across columns
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 49*a(n-1) -450*a(n-2) +1466*a(n-3) -1853*a(n-4) +789*a(n-5) for n>8
This is true. The array grows sideways, so it has to be counted a column at a time, but the clause about which value turns up first is stated in row major order, and a walk across columns does not read the cells in that order. What the walk can carry is, for each named value, the lowest row it has turned up in so far, together with the order those lowest rows were reached; the clause itself is checked only at the end, since a value's lowest row can still drop later. That makes a(n) a walk count on 199 states, so it satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence and checking the one above is a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 8. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A233219  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A233219, proved by carrying a row major clause across columns
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 111*a(n-1) -2128*a(n-2) +10532*a(n-3) -17559*a(n-4) +9045*a(n-5) for n>7
This is true. The array grows sideways, so it has to be counted a column at a time, but the clause about which value turns up first is stated in row major order, and a walk across columns does not read the cells in that order. What the walk can carry is, for each named value, the lowest row it has turned up in so far, together with the order those lowest rows were reached; the clause itself is checked only at the end, since a value's lowest row can still drop later. That makes a(n) a walk count on 324 states, so it satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence and checking the one above is a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 7. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A236519  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 82 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 101 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Its order is 82, the order stated here, and so is the order of every tail. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A239031  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A239031, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(4 - 9*x + 13*x\^{}2 - 11*x\^{}3 + 5*x\^{}4) / (1 - x)\^{}5.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 16 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A239844  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A239844, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(1 - x + x\^{}2)*(3 - 4*x + 4*x\^{}3 - 2*x\^{}4) / (1 - x)\^{}5.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 14 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A240333  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A240333, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(4 - 9*x + 18*x\^{}2 - 18*x\^{}3 + 14*x\^{}4 - 6*x\^{}5 - x\^{}6 + 2*x\^{}7) / (1 - x)\^{}6.
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 22 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A242543  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: Empirical: G.f.: -2*x*(6+4*x+12*x\^{}2+9*x\^{}3) / ( (2*x\^{}2+2*x-1)*(2*x\^{}2+1) ). - \_R. J. Mathar\_, May 18 2014
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 36 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A250654  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A250654, proved
    conjecture: Empirical g.f.: 2*x*(32 - 29*x) / ((1 - x)*(1 - 2*x)). - \_Colin Barker\_, Nov 15 2018
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 128 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A250806  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A250806, proved
    conjecture: Empirical g.f.: x*(100 - 221*x + 141*x\^{}2) / ((1 - x)*(1 - 2*x)*(1 - 3*x)). - \_Colin Barker\_, Nov 20 2018
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 27 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A252970  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: Empirical: G.f.: -x\^{}3*(1+6*x-9*x\^{}2+3*x\^{}3) / (x-1)\^{}7 . - \_R. J. Mathar\_, Nov 23 2015
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 21 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A259216  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A259216, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: x*(13 - 16*x - 16*x\^{}2) / ((1 - 2*x)*(1 - x - x\^{}2)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 9 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A263053  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A263053, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: 2*x / ((1 - x)*(1 - 2*x)*(1 + 2*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 6 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A266063  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 78 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 97 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A267641  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 93 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 2619 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Its order is 93, the order stated here, and so is the order of every tail. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A267867  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1+9*x+100*x\^{}2) / ((1-x)*(1-100*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 4 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A267953  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 56 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 1688 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Its order is 56, the order stated here, and so is the order of every tail. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A269270  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A269270, proved by a counting transfer matrix
    conjecture: \small Empirical: a(n) = 18*a(n-1) - 81*a(n-2).
The empirical recurrence is true. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 32 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 2. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A270086  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (3+4*x+26*x\^{}2-4*x\^{}3-x\^{}4+4*x\^{}5+4*x\^{}6-8*x\^{}7+4*x\^{}9) / ((1-x)\^{}2*(1+x)\^{}3).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 24 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A270257  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A270257, proved by an exact quasi-polynomial
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 2*a(n-1) -2*a(n-3) +a(n-4)
This is true, and the closed form behind it is exact for every n. The shape of the triangle is fixed and it is the alphabet 0..n that grows, so this is not a walk count and no transfer matrix applies. Sum over the sets of adjacent pairs instead: a set of pairs forces the values along each of its connected components to alternate, so a bipartite component has n+1 choices (n for the target n+1) and a component with an odd cycle forces 2x = t, which is possible only for one parity of n. Inclusion-exclusion then gives a(n) = A(n) + (-1)^n C(n) with A and C explicit polynomials, and the recurrence above is exactly (E-1)^(deg A+1) (E+1)^(deg C+1) applied to that, so it holds for every n. The two n mod 2 formulas on this entry are the same statement read at each parity, and are exact as well. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A277560  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1 + 11*x - 101*x\^{}2 + 100*x\^{}4)/((1 - x)*(1 + x)*(1 - 10*x)*(1 + 10*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 7 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A277653  An element and the cells around it: OEIS A
    conjecture: Empirical: a(n) = 3*a(n-1) + 2*a(n-2) - 2*a(n-4).
The empirical recurrence is true. Every cell the condition names lies a bounded number of lines away -- two of them, where it reaches a knight's move -- so a window of that width decides the condition on the line in the middle, and the lines with nothing far enough beyond them are decided at the end. Counting a line at a time therefore gives a transfer matrix with 6 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that; checking the one above is then a finite exact computation, and it holds for n > 4. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

    conjecture: G.f.: (1 - x\^{}2 + 3*x\^{}3)/((1 - x)*(1 + x)*(1 - 2*x)*(1 + 2*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. A278665  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1 +x -99*x\^{}2 -99*x\^{}3 -100*x\^{}4 +9900*x\^{}5 +10000*x\^{}6 -1000000*x\^{}7 +1000000*x\^{}10) / ((1 -x)*(1 +x)*(1 -10*x)*(1 +x\^{}2)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 19 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

    conjecture: G.f.: (1 + 100*x\^{}2 + 10*x\^{}4 + 990*x\^{}6 - 1000*x\^{}10) / ((1 - x)*(1 + x)*(1 - 10*x)*(1 + 10*x)*(1 + 100*x\^{}2)).
The conjectured generating function is correct.     conjecture: G.f.: (2*x\^{}2 + 1)/(4*x\^{}4 - 5*x\^{}2 + 1). (End)
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 6 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. A282002  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1 + 10*x\^{}2)*(1 + 10*x - 100*x\^{}2) / ((1 - x)*(1 + x)*(1 - 10*x)*(1 + 10*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 7 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A283649  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1 - x + 11*x\^{}2 + 1000*x\^{}3 - 12000*x\^{}4 + 11000*x\^{}5) / ((1 - x)*(1 - 10*x)*(1 + 10*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 9 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A284179  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1 + 9*x + 91*x\^{}2 + 909*x\^{}3 - 899*x\^{}4 + 1000*x\^{}5 - 1000*x\^{}6 + 900*x\^{}7 + 90*x\^{}8 + 9*x\^{}9 + x\^{}10 + 10000*x\^{}13 - 10000*x\^{}14) 
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 22 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A286771  The conjectured generating function for OEIS A, proved
    conjecture: G.f.: (1 + x - 101*x\^{}2 + 10*x\^{}3 + 10100*x\^{}4 - 10000*x\^{}6) / ((1 - x)*(1 + x)*(1 - 10*x)*(1 + 10*x)).
The conjectured generating function is correct. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix on 9 states, and the generating function of a walk count is 1/det(I - xM) times a polynomial, so it is a ratio of two polynomials whose degrees are at most the number of states. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

The conjectured expression is another such ratio, of known degree, and two of them are equal as soon as enough coefficients agree: cross-multiplying leaves a polynomial whose degree is bounded, so it vanishes once that many coefficients match. Enough coefficients were compared in exact arithmetic. It follows that a(n) satisfies the linear recurrence whose coefficients are read off the denominator, which this entry does not currently record. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A298708  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 70 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 72 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Its order is 70, the order stated here, and so is the order of every tail. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A301783  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 46 (see link above).
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 51 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. Its order is 46, the order stated here, and so is the order of every tail. Any recurrence of that order the sequence satisfies therefore has the same characteristic polynomial, so it is this one. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A301921  Eventual periodicity modulo $m$ with period dividing $\varphi(m)$:\\a proof of Bala's conjecture on OEIS A301921
    conjecture: \small \textbf{Conjecture:} Let k be a positive integer. The sequence obtained by reducing a(n) modulo k is eventually periodic with the period dividing phi(k) 
This is true. Under t = e^x - 1 the entry's e.g.f. becomes an ordinary power series with integer coefficients; that integrality kills all but finitely many terms of the Stirling expansion of a(n) modulo k, and what is left is an integer combination of the sequences n -> j^n, each eventually periodic mod k with period dividing phi(k). - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A303420  The empirical recurrence for OEIS A: recovering a conjecture that is not written down
    conjecture: Empirical recurrence of order 58 (see link above)
The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. Counting the arrays a row at a time gives a transfer matrix with 119 states, so a(n) satisfies a constant-coefficient linear recurrence of order at most that, and Berlekamp-Massey on exact terms returns the minimal one. This is true. The argument does not manipulate the sequence at all: form the exponential generating function of the right-hand side and exchange the order of summation. The inner sum is then the central binomial series Sum_k C(2k,k) z^k = (1 - 4z)^(-1/2) at z = e^x/6, and 1 - 4*e^x/6 cancels against the 3 - 2e^x, returning the entry's own generating function. The exchange is justified by absolute convergence on |x| < log(3/2), which is exactly the disc where the generating function is analytic. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

    conjecture: \small \textbf{Conjecture:} Let k be a positive integer. The sequence obtained by reducing a(n) modulo k is eventually periodic with the period dividing phi(k) 
This is true. The recurrence in the linked file is correct, and it is the one below. A348410  A proof of the conjectured recurrence for OEIS A348410
    conjecture: \small a(n) = [x\textasciicircum{}n] ( (1 - x)*(1 - x\textasciicircum{}2) )\textasciicircum{}(-n).
The entry posts no generating function, but its definition a(n) = [x^n] f(x)g(x)^n gives one: reading the extraction as a contour integral and summing the geometric series leaves a single integral whose only pole inside a small circle is the branch of x = t*g(x) through the origin, and the residue there is an algebraic function. The recurrence then follows from it, for n > 4. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

A352117  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true for n > 0. Forming the exponential generating function of the right-hand side and exchanging the order of summation turns the inner sum into the central binomial series (1 - 4z)^(-1/2) at z = e^(2x)/8, and 1 - 4*e^(2x)/8 cancels against 2 - e^(2x). What is left over is the k = 0 term, which the summation range excludes, contributing the constant 1/sqrt(2); that affects only the coefficient of x^0, which is exactly why the conjecture has to be stated for n > 0. - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026

This is true, and elementary. A358319  (hand-written; the paper source is gone)
This is true, and elementary. Grouping the summation range by gcd(k,n) converts the sum into a Dirichlet convolution with Euler's totient; at a prime power all but two of the terms are equal and collapse into a single multiple of p^e - p^(e-1). - _Adrian Perez Fontelles_, Sep 06 2026
